text: Cobb modeled the campus on Oxford and Cambridge, the courtyards and the narrow passages and the long sight lines, the crenellations and the gargoyles and the grotesques carved into the stone.
It was new construction made to look six hundred years old.
Chicago was barely sixty years old as a city.
The University of Chicago, two years old, was already dressing itself in the costume of an ancient one.
And the timing was almost theatrical.
As the first buildings went up, the World's Columbian Exposition was being built right next door, in Jackson Park and along the Midway Plaisance, the southern edge of the campus.
The fair opened in 1893, a temporary city of white plaster palaces and the first Ferris wheel, drawing millions of visitors past the new university's gates.
The exposition came down within the year.
In the university's first decade he put in about thirty-five million dollars, an enormous sum for the time.
He later called it the best investment he ever made, and he meant it as money well spent.
The institution that money built did not stay inside its gates.
From the start, it shaped the neighborhood around it, who could buy there, who could rent there, who could live near the quads at all.
The years after the First World War were the years of the Great Migration.
Hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners came north to Chicago looking for work and for distance from Jim Crow.
The city packed most of them into a narrow corridor on the South Side that people called the Black Belt, where the housing was scarce and the rents were high.
By the 1920s, Black families were pressing outward from that corridor, and many of them were heading toward Woodlawn, just across the Midway from campus.
